Which offices touch a Bay County tax bill

A Bay County bill passes through three sets of hands: an assessor in your own township or city, that unit's treasurer, and later, if the bill goes unpaid, the County Treasurer. The county is built on 14 townships and 4 cities, and tax assessment mostly belongs to those local units.

The Equalization Department audits fairness across units. Staff study sales and appraisals class by class in every local unit so that assessments stay near 49 to 50 percent of value countywide. The same office drafts the Millage Reduction Report. Your parcel's individual value is left to the local assessor.

  • Assessor: places the value on your parcel and sends the change notice. The county publishes a contact list covering each township and city.
  • Township or city treasurer: mails the July and December bills and takes the first payment.
  • County Treasurer: picks up delinquent real property tax, certifies deeds, and chairs the Land Bank Authority.
  • Equalization: keeps parcel ownership and land description records for most of Bay County. Bangor Township, Hampton Township, Bay City and Essexville keep their own descriptions.

Due dates and where to pay

Bills go out in July and again in December from the township or city treasurer. Any balance that remains with that local treasurer after February 28 is handed to the County Treasurer, and MCL 211.78 sets the rules for collecting it from there.

The County Treasurer's counter is on the sixth floor of the Bay County Building, 515 Center Ave., downtown Bay City. Staff are there weekdays, 8 a.m. through 5 p.m., and the main number is 989-895-4285.

Do not email card numbers or ACH forms, since email is not secure. Mail, fax or phone them in.

How to appeal your valuation

Your first stop is the local board of review. State law (MCL 211.30) schedules its opening session for the second Monday of March, though a township or city may choose the Tuesday or Wednesday that follows. During that week the board has to hold at least 12 hours of hearings, including three evening hours after 6 p.m.

Anyone who files a protest must receive a written outcome by the first Monday in June, along with a notice about going further to the Michigan Tax Tribunal. For a house, a tribunal petition is due on July 31 of the tax year. Commercial and industrial owners face May 31 (MCL 205.735a). A homeowner generally has to raise the issue at the board of review before the tribunal will take it.

  • Phone your unit's assessor and ask whether a letter protest is allowed in place of an appearance.
  • Pick up your appraisal record card from the township or city, because those cards are kept locally.
  • Use Equalization for parcel ownership, descriptions and tax data. It is staffed Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. through 4 p.m.

A dispute over a principal residence exemption starts at the July or December board of review, then may reach the tribunal.

Disabled veteran exemption and payment trouble

A disabled veteran exemption is available. A veteran needs only one of three qualifications: a federal ruling of permanent and total service connected disability paid at 100 percent, a certificate showing aid for specially adapted housing, or an unemployability rating.

The unremarried surviving spouse keeps the benefit as long as that spouse lives in Michigan. Each year the owner files an affidavit and the federal documents with the local assessor. The filing window opens on tax day and closes when the local board of review adjourns for good.

If you cannot cover a bill, call the County Treasurer before the February 28 handoff and ask what options exist. The Land Bank Authority is another resource. The Board of Commissioners created it on August 11, 2009 to take on odd property problems and parcels that do not sell at a public auction.

Selling with taxes owed

Back taxes stay with the land, so a seller settles them at or before the closing table. Under MCL 211.135 the register of deeds asks for tax certification on warranty deeds, land contracts and condominium master deeds, showing five years of paid tax before the instrument date. Bay County's certificate costs $5, handed over on its own check to the County Treasurer.

A quitclaim deed without a warranty covenant is excused from that step. Even so, most lenders and title companies still want the tax history clean. Have the closing agent request a payoff from the treasurer ahead of the signing date.

For parcels in delinquency, the county treasurer is the foreclosing governmental unit. MCL 211.78 says forfeited property can face a foreclosure judgment if nobody redeems it. An owner with arrears should call the treasurer well before any notice shows up.

Transfer tax at recording

Recording the deed also brings transfer tax. The Register of Deeds charges $7.50 for every $1,000 of price to the state and $1.10 per $1,000 to the county. Ask your closing agent to add both to the settlement statement so the number is not a surprise at the table.

The usual sequence is simple. The title company orders the tax search, the treasurer issues the $5 certificate if the deed needs one, you sign, and the closing agent sends the deed for recording with the tax. A cash buyer who takes the house as-is follows the same path but skips lender repair demands.

Bay County housing at a glance

Bay County has 102,123 residents in 2025, 1.7 percent fewer than the April 2020 base. Housing totals 48,704 units for 45,103 households, and owners live in 77.0 percent of occupied homes. The 2020 to 2024 median home value is $152,200. Mortgage holders spend a median $1,249 a month on housing costs, against $557 for owners with no loan. Nearly one resident in four, 24.2 percent, is 65 or older, so exemption timing and downsizing sales come up often.

Frequently asked questions

After what date do Bay County property taxes move to the county?

A balance still open with the township or city treasurer on February 28 passes to the Bay County Treasurer, under MCL 211.78. Call 989-895-4285 to get a payoff number.

Can I pay a Bay County property tax bill online?

Yes. The County Treasurer takes cards on its website with a 3% fee. Mail, phone, wire, counter, drop box and standing ACH debits are accepted too.

Who decides what my Bay County house is worth for tax purposes?

Your township or city assessor makes that call. The county Equalization Department only tests whether assessments across units stay close to 49 to 50 percent.

How long do I have to take a homestead valuation to the Tax Tribunal?

For residential property the petition is due July 31 of the tax year, after the board of review protest. Commercial and industrial petitions are due May 31 under MCL 205.735a.

Must a Bay County deed carry a tax certificate?

Warranty deeds, land contracts and condominium master deeds do, and it costs $5 on a separate check to the County Treasurer. A quitclaim deed with no warranty is excused under MCL 211.135.

Who handles property tax in Calhoun County

Responsibility is divided among the local assessor, the local board of review and the County Treasurer in Marshall. The treasurer's office, in the County Building at 315 West Green Street, collects real estate taxes that go delinquent and manages reversion of unpaid parcels through title searches, property visits, court hearings, foreclosure and auction. It also issues deed certifications and helps run the Calhoun County Land Bank.

  • Delinquent taxes, hardship extensions, deed certification: 269-781-0807.
  • Homestead and taxable value changes: 269-781-0808.
  • Land bank: 269-781-0777.
  • Counter opens at 8 a.m. daily, closes at 5 p.m. Monday through Thursday and at noon on Friday.

Ask the assessor in your city or township about the value of a given parcel, and ask the treasurer or the mailing unit about the millage on your bill.

How taxable value is set

Assessments run at 50% of true cash value. The figure the millage multiplies is taxable value, which may climb each year by no more than the smaller of 5% or inflation and never past state equalized value, under MCL 211.27a. When ownership transfers, the next year's taxable value snaps back to state equalized value.

Sellers should warn buyers about that snap-back. A house held down by years of capped increases can produce a noticeably bigger bill for its new owner. A buyer with questions about the post-sale bill can call the treasurer's taxable value line, 269-781-0808.

Tax calendar

These dates are set in Michigan statute and recur each year for every Calhoun County parcel.

Annual Michigan tax milestones for Calhoun County owners
StepRule

Principal residence exemptionAffidavit due June 1 to catch the summer bill, November 1 for the winter bill

Commercial and industrial petitions to the tribunal are due a bit sooner, on May 31.

How to challenge an assessment

Begin at the March board of review. A residential owner has to protest there before the Michigan Tax Tribunal will hear the case, and the board owes a written decision, with notice of appeal rights, by the first Monday in June. A nonresident taxpayer can send the protest and supporting papers by letter instead of appearing.

If the board leaves the value alone, the petition to the tribunal is due July 31 for residential and farm property. Postmark, hand delivery or handoff to a designated delivery service by the deadline counts as timely. Serve a copy on the local assessor by certified mail. You can argue your own case or send an attorney or other representative.

A denied principal residence exemption goes first to the July or December board of review. The governing statutes are MCL 211.30 and MCL 205.735a.

Relief for owners behind on taxes

Homeowners working to catch up on forfeited taxes can apply to the treasurer for a financial hardship extension. It pushes the foreclosure deadline back by as much as a year, in return for a payment plan. The extension covers only the time to pay: 1.5% monthly interest, fees and penalties keep accruing, so the debt keeps growing. Apply online, then expect a call to set an appointment. The number is 269-781-0807.

  • Disabled service members: an honorably discharged Michigan resident who is rated permanently and totally disabled at 100% by the VA, holds a VA certificate for specially adapted housing, or is rated individually unemployable. Surviving spouses can qualify. File the State Tax Commission affidavit with the local assessor each year.
  • Principal residence exemption: file an affidavit with the local tax collecting unit under MCL 211.7cc.
  • Foreclosure auctions: the treasurer's document center carries auction results for 2013 through 2025, which shows what tax-foreclosed parcels brought.

Once a parcel has gone through foreclosure, ask the treasurer how the reversion timeline will run before an auction is scheduled.

Selling with taxes owed

Taxes follow the property into a sale. The summer bill becomes a lien and falls due July 1, and tax collected after the payable deadline picks up a 4% county fee plus interest at 1% per month, under MCL 211.44. Anything unpaid on March 1 is sent to the county treasurer. The treasurer's website offers pages to look up and pay delinquent taxes, so an owner can see a balance before listing.

For a warranty deed, MCL 211.135 requires the county treasurer to certify that no tax liens or titles are held and that five years of taxes are paid. The Register of Deeds charges $5 for the certification. Arrange payoff through the title company early enough for the certificate to issue before the closing date.

Here is the order that works. Call 269-781-0807 for the balance, give the figure to the title company, and let it be paid out of your proceeds at closing. A cash sale that skips lender requirements still needs the certificate for a warranty deed. If the balance has already gone to the county, ask the treasurer whether the figure includes the fee and monthly interest, so the payoff you plan around matches the one the title company sees on closing day.

Who sends your bill

Bills come from the local unit where the parcel sits. The county has four cities, Albion, Battle Creek, Marshall and Springfield, and five villages: Athens, Burlington, Homer, Tekonsha and Union City. Sixteen townships complete the list: Albion, Athens, Burlington, Clarence, Clarendon, Convis, Eckford, Fredonia, Homer, Lee, Leroy, Marengo, Marshall, Newton, Sheridan and Tekonsha.

Whichever unit you live in, the same county treasurer handles taxes after they go delinquent, and the same state calendar applies. Keep each bill and notice in one folder. When you list the house, the title company will want the most recent summer and winter bills, and the assessor's notice if you have it, so it can confirm the taxable value and any exemption on the parcel.

Calhoun County housing at a glance

The county's 2025 estimate is 133,408 residents. Battle Creek is the biggest city, and Marshall is the seat. The middle owner-occupied home is valued at $162,800. Selected monthly owner costs run $1,271 with a mortgage and $545 without. Builders took out 120 permits in 2025.

Frequently asked questions

Which treasurer collects property tax in Calhoun County?

Your city or township treasurer sends the regular bill, and the County Treasurer takes over once taxes are returned delinquent. The county office is at 315 West Green Street in Marshall, phone 269-781-0807.

When does the Calhoun County board of review meet?

It convenes the second Monday in March, or the Tuesday or Wednesday after if the local unit chooses, and meets 12 hours or more that week. Your assessor can give you the local schedule.

What is the filing deadline for the Michigan Tax Tribunal?

For residential, agricultural and timber-cutover real property it is July 31 of the tax year, and for commercial, industrial and developmental property it is May 31. A residential owner must protest to the board of review first.

Can the Calhoun County Treasurer postpone a tax foreclosure?

For homeowners, yes. A financial hardship extension can delay the foreclosure deadline up to one year when a payment plan is in place, though 1.5% monthly interest and fees continue to accrue.

Are Calhoun County property taxes settled at closing?

Normally the title company clears any balance from the sale. Before a warranty deed can be recorded, the county treasurer must certify paid taxes, and the Register of Deeds charges $5 for that.

Who does what on a Genesee County tax bill

Three layers share the work. A city or township assessor values each parcel, a local treasurer collects the current bill, and the county treasurer steps in once the balance is overdue on March 1. In between, the county equalization office audits the local assessors so that values stay comparable across the county.

Flint is the county seat, and 33 cities, townships and villages share the county. The eleven cities are Burton, Clio, Davison, Fenton (partly in the county), Flint, Flushing, Grand Blanc, Linden, Montrose, Mount Morris and Swartz Creek. Gaines, Goodrich, Lennon, Otisville and Otter Lake are villages. Your parcel's municipality decides which assessor and local treasurer you call.

Flint is the one exception to county record keeping. Equalization maintains property descriptions for every municipality but Flint, whose own assessor keeps those records.

County offices and where to find them

Three county offices fit this topic, all inside the county administration building on South Saginaw Street in Flint. Owners go to the city or township for assessments and current bills, and to the county only for delinquent ones.

  • Equalization, Suite 8B: (810) 257-3017. It writes the annual equalization report and the millage reduction report.
  • Treasurer, Suite 2A, 324 S Saginaw St: (810) 257-3054, weekdays from 8:00 to 4:00. It takes delinquent payments and runs tax foreclosure. Partial payments are encouraged, by mail, online or through an automated line at 1-877-805-2856, and the online and phone routes add a fee.
  • Clerk and Register of Deeds, Suite 1A: records deeds and mortgages. See the separate register of deeds guide for its fees and transfer tax.

State Tax Commission Bulletin 11 of 2025 lays out the 2026 property tax, collections and equalization calendar for local officials.

Genesee County housing market

With 401,093 residents in the 2025 estimate, Genesee has lost 1.3% since the April 2020 base. It counts 167,334 households and 185,007 housing units, and owners live in 70.7% of occupied homes.

  • Median home value: $182,400 for 2020-2024.
  • Monthly ownership cost: $1,455 with a mortgage, $583 without.
  • Median gross rent: $989.
  • Median household income: $62,281.
  • Building permits in 2025: 444.

Before you set a price, check which municipality's assessor holds your parcel and ask for the record card, because taxable value and sale price are different numbers. Bills follow those values, so a Flint homeowner, where the median is $53,500, sees a very different tax picture from a Grand Blanc one. Each city, township or village bills its current tax through its own treasurer, so first confirm which municipality your parcel is in.

Where a Genesee County owner can contest a value

At the local board of review in the owner's own city or township, then at the Michigan Tax Tribunal. The county does not hear individual appeals.

Each board convenes on the second Monday of March unless the local government shifts the first sitting to the Tuesday or Wednesday after. Over that week a board owes the public at least 12 hours, three of them after 6 p.m. Each person who protests receives written word of the outcome by the first Monday of June, with the tribunal's address and filing date. Out-of-town owners can protest by letter.

Tribunal petitions are due May 31 for commercial, industrial and developmental real property and July 31 for residential and farm property, and a residential owner must have gone to the board first. Boards also sit in July and December for qualified errors, such as a clerical slip or a wrong measurement, and for certain exemptions. Those fixes reach back only to the current and previous year. If you spot an error in your record card, don't wait for March, since these later sittings exist for exactly that.

How a Genesee County bill becomes delinquent

Whatever is still unpaid on March 1 of the year after the levy goes to the Genesee County Treasurer, which serves as the county's foreclosing unit. This is the schedule Michigan Treasury sets.

Genesee County delinquent tax schedule

March 1, year oneCharges a 4% fee plus 1% monthly interest on unpaid bills
June 1 and September 1Sends two first-class mailings to the owner
October 1Adds a $15 fee
February 1, year twoSends certified mail to the owner and a letter to the occupant
March 1, year twoForfeits the parcel, adds a $175 title fee, starts half-percent monthly redemption interest
March 30 and 31, year threeJudgment deadline, then the last day to redeem

Sales then happen online. The county runs a minimum bid auction, a re-offer round and a no-reserve sale each fall. A Genesee County Land Bank exists to help return foreclosed property to the tax rolls.

Money left over from a foreclosure sale

Sometimes a former owner can claim it. For sales on or after July 18, 2020, an owner or lienholder files Form 5743, the Notice of Intention to Claim Interest in Foreclosure Sales Proceeds, and then a motion to claim the remaining proceeds on form CC 540. Both forms sit on the treasurer's page, along with the State Bar of Michigan referral line, 800-968-0738.

Call the treasurer's office first, and ask plainly whether any proceeds are held for your parcel. Bring the parcel number, proof that you owned the property at the time of the sale, and any lien paperwork you hold, so staff can point you to the right form. If you aren't sure how to file the motion, the referral line above can connect you with a lawyer.

Selling when tax is still owed

The closing agent obtains a payoff, and the unpaid tax, interest and fees are deducted from the seller's check. If the bill has been returned to the county, the payoff comes from the county treasurer's office.

Sellers also owe transfer tax, which runs $4.30 for each $500 of price: $3.75 for the state and 55 cents for the county. It is due to the county treasurer inside 15 days of delivery. A few transfers, such as family gifts and foreclosure deeds, are exempt.

Owners who are behind, or who hold a house in poor repair, can sell for cash as-is and have the payoff handled at the closing table. Before you list, check these points:

  1. Which municipality holds your parcel, and whether the current bill is paid.
  2. Whether the balance has moved to the county treasurer, and the payoff amount there.
  3. Whether any partial payment plan with the county is open.
  4. What your title company needs to show a clear tax history at closing.

Frequently asked questions

Which office takes delinquent Genesee County property tax?

The Genesee County Treasurer, 324 S Saginaw St Ste 2A in Flint, takes payments by mail, online or phone. Staff are at the counter on weekdays, and the online and phone options carry a fee.

Does the county decide what my property is worth?

No, the assessor of your city or township does. Equalization only checks that local assessments are comparable countywide and calculates the millage reduction report.

Is there a Tax Tribunal deadline for a home?

Yes. A residential petition is due July 31 of the tax year, after a protest at the local board. Commercial and industrial petitions are due May 31.

How soon can Genesee County foreclose over unpaid tax?

The process spans about three years. The parcel forfeits on the second March 1, a judgment must come by March 30 of year three, and March 31 is the last day to redeem.

What is the total transfer tax rate in Genesee County?

The seller pays $4.30 on each $500 of price, made up of $3.75 for the state and 55 cents for the county. Payment goes to the county treasurer inside 15 days of delivery.

Where to take a property tax question in Bad Axe

Start in the county building at 250 East Huron Avenue, Bad Axe, MI 48413. The Treasurer sits in Room 204 (989-269-9238). Equalization is in Room 306 (989-269-6497), and Tax Mapping and GIS shares Room 306 (989-269-9421). Both offices post weekday hours from half past eight to half past four, with no lunch closure at the Treasurer's desk.

Valuation work happens nearer the house. In Michigan the assessing job belongs to each city or township, so whoever sets your value works for the unit that contains the house. The county home page links an Assessing and Tax Search page and a FetchGIS parcel map, and the Treasurer's page adds that the Huron County Land Bank runs out of the Treasurer's office.

Does my township or the county send the bill?

Your local collector sends the first bill. MCL 211.44 has the township treasurer or other collector mail a statement listing the parcel description, taxable value and tax due. Missing the mailing does not wipe out the tax. Anything unpaid as of March 1 is returned to the county treasurer, and the law has the collector note that return on the statement.

Huron County does some of the collecting itself. Its Treasurer takes ACH payments toward delinquent taxes and toward the summer taxes of the City of Harbor Beach and Grant Township. Fill in the authorization form and post it to PO Box 69, Bad Axe, MI 48413, or ring 989-269-9238 and finish the form by phone. Plastic is accepted too, at a 3 percent surcharge. Since the collecting office varies by unit, learn who holds your parcel's bill before you pay anyone.

Late charges and penalties

The charges step up with the calendar, and a local governing body can trim them. These come from MCL 211.44:

  • An administration fee of as much as 1 percent can be tacked on to a bill settled ahead of February 15 the next year.
  • After that, up to the delinquency date, the city or township may authorize a 3 percent late penalty.
  • Interest then builds at 1 percent monthly.
  • Any unpaid administration fee travels with the bill to the county treasurer.

The statute lets a governing body waive part of these charges for seniors and certain other groups. The office that mailed your bill can say whether you qualify.

Will the buyer pay more tax than I do?

Often, yes. Between sales, a parcel's taxable value may rise each year by no more than 5 percent or the inflation rate, whichever is lower, and never past state equalized value. A transfer of ownership ends the cap. MCL 211.27a sets the taxable value in the year after a transfer equal to state equalized value, a figure aimed at 50 percent of true cash value.

A conveyance by deed counts as a transfer. So a Huron County farmhouse owned for decades under a capped figure can carry a noticeably bigger bill in the first year for its new owner. Tell the buyer to budget for it, and expect the question when you show the house.

How to appeal your assessment

A residential or farm owner goes to the local board of review first, then to the Michigan Tax Tribunal, with a petition due July 31 of that tax year. Commercial and industrial owners have until May 31. The rules in MCL 205.735a set these dates.

A fight over a principal residence exemption has to reach the July or December board of review before the Tribunal can take it. The local assessor knows when those boards sit.

Which local units bill Huron County owners?

Huron County has three cities, Bad Axe, Caseville and Harbor Beach, plus the unincorporated community of Bay Port and a ring of townships. Each unit assesses property inside its borders, and the first bill normally comes from the local collector. The county's part is to equalize values among the units, take in what goes delinquent and keep the parcel mapping. Grant Township is the one township the Treasurer's page names for summer tax payments, alongside the City of Harbor Beach, whose summer bills can be paid through the county office.

A lakefront cottage near Port Austin and a field near Bad Axe can sit in different units with different local levies. Ask the unit that mails your bill for its millage rate sheet.

Build a brief checklist and take it to the Treasurer and to your township or city office. Call 989-269-9238 and ask the parcel's standing, including delinquent sums sent to the county. For a warranty deed, ask whether a tax certificate is required at recording.

Keep each bill and receipt for the title company. If the Land Bank ever handled the parcel, ask what is of record. Value questions go to the assessor, and Equalization in Room 306 can name the right local unit.

Selling with taxes owed

Unpaid taxes do not stop you from selling, but the balance has to be cleared at closing. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff, hand it to the title company, and the amount comes out of your proceeds. If the bill has already gone to the county on March 1, only the county Treasurer can quote it. Sellers who would rather skip repairs, showings and a buyer's financing delays sometimes choose a cash sale, which still needs the same payoff and tax certificate steps before the deed records.

Housing in Huron County

Huron County fills the Thumb's northern tip, with an economy built on farming. A typical owner-occupied house is valued at $154,300, and owners live in 81.8 percent of homes. Median gross rent is $788. Monthly owner costs are $1,135 with a mortgage and $510 without. Population dropped from 31,407 in 2020 to an estimated 30,530 in 2025, so buyers have plenty of choice and modest prices are the norm. Pricing the house with that in mind, and having the tax picture ready, tends to make showings go more smoothly.

Where can I pay overdue taxes in Huron County?

Walk them into Room 204 at 250 East Huron Avenue, or mail them to PO Box 69, Bad Axe, MI 48413. An ACH authorization form is available for delinquent taxes, and cards add a 3 percent fee.

When do unpaid taxes move to the Huron County treasurer?

On March 1. Taxes still open that day are handed to the county treasurer under MCL 211.44.

Does selling raise the next owner's bill in Huron County?

Usually. Under MCL 211.27a a transfer of ownership resets taxable value to state equalized value in the following year, which can be well above the capped figure on a home held for a long time.

July 31 for residential property, after a board of review protest. Commercial and industrial parcels have until May 31.

Whom you pay for property tax

Start with your local city or township, which issues and collects the regular bill. The Jackson County Treasurer steps in only after a bill goes delinquent. A homeowner who is current writes the check to the local unit, while an owner who has slipped behind pays the county office instead.

Jackson is the county's only city and the seat. Its villages are Brooklyn, Cement City (partly in the county), Concord, Grass Lake, Hanover, Parma and Springport, and townships cover the remainder. Each local unit bills its own residents, so before listing a house, confirm which unit sends yours.

What happens when a bill becomes delinquent?

Once a bill is delinquent it moves to the County Treasurer, and from then on payments go to that office alone. In the first delinquent month the charge is a 4 percent penalty plus 1 percent interest. After that, interest runs 1 percent monthly. Taxes left unpaid beyond a year carry a higher rate and extra fees.

The same office collects delinquent personal property tax for 18 units and runs the Delinquent Tax Revolving Fund, a pool that keeps cities, townships, villages, schools and the junior college whole while the county pursues what is owed. Tax certification for a deed

Look at your assessing record before you list, since it shows what the local assessor holds on the house. If something looks off, take it to the city or township assessor, because assessing in Michigan is mostly a local job.

Selling lifts the cap on taxable value. Michigan Treasury says the uncapping takes effect in the calendar year after the transfer of ownership, so a buyer can expect a bill closer to assessed value. When does a Jackson County property tax bill become delinquent?

Once February ends, whatever remains unpaid turns delinquent and moves to the County Treasurer. The first month adds a 4 percent penalty and 1 percent interest, and later months add 1 percent.

No. You pay current bills to your city or township, and delinquent ones to the Treasurer. Inside the City of Jackson the summer bill is due by July 31, or in five installments.

Call (855) 246-9331 and give your parcel ID. The phone fee is 3 percent with a $2.00 floor, and online card payments also carry 3 percent.

The owner is responsible for telling the local township or city that no bill came. Call that office promptly.

Who bills and collects the tax

Your city or township sends the bill. The county treasurer gets involved only when a bill goes unpaid. Kent's Bureau of Equalization keeps assessments uniform across 21 townships and nine cities, and your local assessor sets the value on your own parcel.

That split tells you whom to call. A wrong value, a missing exemption or a bill that never arrived goes to the local assessor or treasurer. A balance returned unpaid, and any foreclosure auction after a court order, belongs to the Kent County Treasurer. The counter is on the first floor of the county building at 300 Monroe Avenue NW in Grand Rapids, open weekdays from 8 am to 5 pm.

Kent County at a glance for sellers

Grand Rapids is the county seat and its largest city. The county has 675,232 residents and 256,648 households. Owners occupy 70.3% of homes. The typical home value is $289,900, median household income is $82,631, and median gross rent is $1,243.

With a typical home near $290,000, a late balance grows into real money fast, since the penalties below are percentages of the unpaid bill. City and township parcels share one collection calendar.

Delinquency dates and penalties

Local treasurers mail bills on July 1 and December 1. A balance still open on the next March 1 passes to the county treasurer, who adds a 4% fee and charges 1% interest each month. None of these charges can be waived, even when an owner's bill never arrived.

Summer bills have an earlier pinch point: MCL 211.44a starts interest on summer tax on September 15. After March 1, the county follows a fixed calendar:

How to pay delinquent taxes

You can pay online, by phone, by mail, through the Kent County mobile app, or at the counter. Keep the parcel number or street address handy.

  • In person: The counter is meant for transactions that require cash. Everyone else is encouraged to pay online or by mail.

Partial payments are accepted at any time, though charges keep running on what remains. Postmarks do not count. A payment has to arrive before the end of a month to be applied at that month's payoff figure, so call 616-632-7500 for the current payoff before you mail a check.

Hardship deferral

An owner who qualifies and applies in time can get up to one year. To qualify for the Financial Hardship program you must hold title by recorded deed or land contract, live in the property as your principal residence, and document a substantial hardship.

The application asks for a payment plan on page 3. A plan can include regular payments or a record of them, help from a local assistance agency, or the sale or refinancing of the property. The form must be in before March 1, and approval is not promised. A deferral is a one-time tool and does not reduce the bill: interest and fees keep piling up during the extension.

The Principal Residence Exemption and the local hardship exemption for low income owners are the two most owners ask about. The PRE removes the local school operating levy, up to 18 mills, from a home you own and live in. File with the local assessor. The cutoffs are June 1 for the summer bill and November 1 for the winter bill.

A PRE denial from the state goes to the Michigan Department of Treasury for an informal conference. A denial from the local unit or county goes to the Michigan Tax Tribunal. Questions about the low income exemption go to the city or township assessor. The homestead property tax credit is separate and is claimed on the Michigan income tax return.

One warning from the treasurer: escrow does not make you safe. A mortgage servicer can miss a payment after a refinance, and you are still the one responsible for checking that the bill was paid.

Selling with taxes owed

A Kent County sale can record cleanly only if the tax history is in order. Before a warranty deed records, the treasurer certifies the parcel's tax status for a $5 fee. MCL 211.135 requires five years of taxes to be paid. A quitclaim deed with no warranty covenants is excepted.

The sale also changes the next bill. The buyer's first full-year bill is figured on the state equalized value instead of your capped taxable value (MCL 211.27a), so expect it to differ from yours.

If you owe a delinquent balance, the closing office requests a payoff from the treasurer and subtracts it from your proceeds. Call 616-632-7500 for a payoff before you choose a closing day. A cash buyer who closes fast can settle the balance before more interest and fees stack up.

When does interest start on unpaid property tax in Kent County?

Summer tax collects interest from September 15 under MCL 211.44a. After March 1 the county's 4% fee and monthly 1% interest apply, and none of those charges can be waived.

How long before the county can foreclose for unpaid taxes?

About two years and one month. Taxes become delinquent March 1, the property is forfeited the following March 1, and foreclosure preparation begins March 31 after that. After a court order, the treasurer sells parcels that have been delinquent more than 24 months.

Does the hardship deferral lower what I owe?

No. It moves the foreclosure deadline back by a year at most. Interest and fees continue to build, and the application has to be in before March 1 with a plan for paying the taxes.

Who do I call to fight my assessment?

Your local assessor first. Valuation complaints go to the local March board of review, and the Michigan Tax Tribunal takes it from there.

Do I have to pay back taxes before I sell?

Usually yes, and the payoff is subtracted from your proceeds at closing. A warranty deed needs a certificate that five years of tax are paid.

Who bills you for property tax

Your township, city or village treasurer sends the bill. The county treasurer steps in only when a bill goes unpaid. The summer bill is dated July 1 and the winter bill December 1, and whatever remains open after March 1 is handed to the Lapeer County Treasurer as delinquent.

Lapeer County is in the Thumb. The City of Lapeer is the county seat, with Imlay City and Brown City as the other two cities. The villages are Almont, Clifford, Columbiaville, Dryden, Metamora, North Branch and Otter Lake, and eighteen townships fill in the rest. Each unit runs its own treasurer and assessor, so the first call about a bill goes to the office for the place where the house sits.

  • Questions about a current bill: the local treasurer. The county treasurer cannot waive local penalties or interest.
  • Value, classification or a principal residence claim: the local assessor.
  • Taxes that turned delinquent after March 1: the County Treasurer in the County Complex at 255 Clay Street, Lapeer.
  • Getting a prior owner's name off a bill: the local assessor, with a deed or other proof of the transfer.

The county equalization office

This office checks that assessments are fair between local units. It does not set the assessment on any one house. The department advises the Board of Commissioners on true cash value and runs annual sales and appraisal studies for each class of property.

That work rests on section 211.34 of the General Property Tax Act, which tells the county board to review each township and city roll for uniformity every year. If your own assessed value looks wrong, take it to the local assessor first. The county office exists to correct gaps between units, such as one township running below the sales level of its neighbors. Public hearings on county operating millage are held in the Commission Chambers at the County Complex.

Late fees and interest

A late bill picks up a flat administration fee and monthly interest, and the county treasurer has no power to waive them.

ChargeAmountWhen it applies

The office takes personal checks, cashier's checks, money orders, credit cards and cash, with checks payable to Lapeer County Treasurer. You can send partial payments whenever you like, and a receipt comes back to the return address. Fees and interest keep running on whatever balance remains.

Mortgage servicers sometimes miss a payment. The owner, not the lender, carries the responsibility, so compare each mortgage statement with the local treasurer's records.

How tax foreclosure works

Foreclosure can begin once taxes are two years delinquent, and the county treasurer then sells the property at public auction. A 1999 law, Public Act 123 (MCL 211.78), cut the time owners have to catch up on unpaid bills.

Forfeiture falls on March 1, one year after the turnover date, and it only prepares the parcel for foreclosure. The property is not lost at forfeiture. The later foreclosure is final, and nothing returns the house to the owner afterward.

  • State law requires five notices: two by first class mail, two by certified mail and one by personal service. The county sends another three to five on its own.
  • Names and addresses of delinquent owners are published in the newspaper, and recorded lienholders, mortgage holders and land contract holders are notified.
  • At the first auction the minimum bid equals all taxes, interest and fees. If a parcel does not sell, a very low minimum applies at the second auction.
  • The foreclosure list is normally available around May 1 each year. Mortgage foreclosures are not run by this office.

Anyone behind on taxes who wants to sell should do it before forfeiture, because the $175 and $60 charges and the higher interest rate arrive on that date.

How to appeal your assessment

Begin at the March board of review in the township, city or village where the house stands. Each unit sets its own meeting dates, so call the local assessor.

For residential property the board of review comes first. Under MCL 205.735a, you then petition the Michigan Tax Tribunal no later than July 31 of the assessment year. Commercial and industrial real property can go straight to the Tribunal, with a May 31 filing date. A petition over an arithmetic error on a bill has its own 60 day limit. Owners representing themselves may appear without an attorney.

Homestead exemption and relief

The principal residence exemption is the main one for homeowners. It lifts the school district operating levy, up to 18 mills, from a residence that a Michigan resident owns and lives in.

  • Form 2368 goes to the local assessor. Filing cutoffs are June 1 ahead of summer billing and November 1 ahead of winter billing.
  • A denied claim can go to an informal conference with the Department of Treasury's exemption unit, or to the Tax Tribunal.
  • The low income hardship exemption is requested at the city or township assessor's office.
  • The county treasurer also accepts financial hardship deferral applications. Ask that office what documents it wants.

The principal residence exemption is separate from the Homestead Property Tax Credit, which is filed with the Michigan income tax return.

What a seller owes at closing

Transfer tax is the seller's cost, collected when the deed is recorded. The county and the state each charge a rate on the sale price, and the Register of Deeds can quote both before you close.

A deed with a covenant of warranty, or a land contract, also needs the County Treasurer's $5 certification under MCL 211.135, and recording adds $30. How the current year's bill is prorated depends on the purchase agreement and the settlement statement prepared by the title company. If an earlier year is delinquent, request a payoff figure from the County Treasurer before closing so the interest and fees are counted correctly.

A cash buyer can close quickly and pay off a delinquent balance at the table, which stops the monthly interest from growing. Whoever you sell to, get the payoff in writing first, and keep the receipt from the treasurer with your closing papers so there is a record that the account is current.

Frequently asked questions

When do Lapeer County property taxes go delinquent?

Unpaid summer and winter bills turn delinquent after March 1 and move to the Lapeer County Treasurer. That is also the day the 4% administration fee is added and 1% monthly interest is counted from the original due date.

Can the county treasurer waive penalties?

No. The fees and interest in the property tax act have no waiver provision, and the office cannot remove them. Ask about the financial hardship deferral if a one-time expense caused the delay.

May I pay a late bill in installments?

Yes. Send any amount at any time, and a receipt comes back by mail. Statutory fees and interest still apply to whatever is left unpaid.

How long before the county can foreclose on unpaid taxes?

Two years from the delinquency. Forfeiture comes a year after turnover on March 1, and foreclosure follows after the notices are served. Foreclosed parcels go to public auction.

Who removes my name from the bill after a sale?

The local assessor in the township, city or village where the house is. The county treasurer has no authority to change a name on a bill, so bring the deed or proof of transfer to the assessor.

Who collects property tax in Lenawee County?

Your local city, village or township treasurer collects the current bill, and the Lenawee County Treasurer takes over once a bill is delinquent. On March 1 each year the county treasurer receives all delinquent taxes from the townships and cities through a step called settlement, and the local units are made whole from the county's Delinquent Tax Fund.

The county treasurer does not collect winter taxes for the current year until they turn delinquent on March 1. Your local treasurer takes payments through the end of February. The county office is on North Main Street in Adrian (mailing address 301 N. Main Street, Adrian, MI 49221). Call 517-264-4554. Hours are Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to noon and 1:00 p.m. to 4:30 p.m.

  • Current bill questions go to the township, city or village treasurer.
  • Delinquent bills, tax certification and land split sign-off go to the county treasurer.
  • Value and taxable value questions start with the assessor, and the county Equalization Department answers at 517-264-4522 on the first floor of the Old Courthouse.

If you are unsure which office holds your bill, start with the parcel number. Winter taxes are due to the local treasurer through the end of February, and anything unpaid after that moves to the county treasurer on March 1, where the balance is handled under the delinquent tax process.

Lenawee County housing and parcel numbers

Lenawee County sits in southeast Michigan along the Ohio line, with Adrian as the county seat. The 2020 census counted 99,423 residents and 43,577 housing units, and 77.3% of occupied homes were owner occupied. Housing ranges from city lots in Adrian, Tecumseh, Hudson and Morenci to lake homes around Manitou Beach and Devils Lake and rural parcels across the townships.

Parcel numbers carry a code for the taxing unit. In the 2026 sale notice, keys starting XA0 belong to the City of Adrian, MD0 to Madison Township and FAW to Weston Village, so the first letters of a parcel number tell you which local office issues the bill.

Paying your bill

You can pay online through the county's BS&A portal, or in person, by mail or by phone for delinquent bills. The county's assessment page walks through the online steps.

  • Open the county's online service and choose Property and Land Search.
  • Search by parcel number, address or owner name in "Smith, John" form.
  • Register an account, confirm the parcel from the email, then log back in and select Pay My Taxes.
  • At the counter, the treasurer accepts cash, check, cashier's check, money order and credit or debit cards. Cards carry an enhanced access fee.

Homeowners who cannot manage the summer bill can ask about the State of Michigan's summer tax deferment. The treasurer's FAQ links to the state's requirements and its application.

Take it to the local board of review in March, then, for a home, to the Michigan Tax Tribunal by July 31. The assessor in your city or township can tell you the board's meeting dates.

The county's assessment page answers the questions owners ask most, such as why an assessment changed when nothing was done to the property, what happens to taxable value after a purchase and how assessed value, state equalized value and taxable value differ. MCL 205.735a sets July 31 for residential and agricultural property and May 31 for commercial and industrial. Other determinations carry a 35 day window from the final decision. For a home, the March board of review must hear the protest first, so a missed March meeting usually ends the appeal for that year.

Tax certification for a sale or land split

The treasurer certifies that taxes are paid in full for the past five years, as MCL 211.135 allows. That certificate is needed on deeds, land contracts and property splits.

  • The office compares the deed's legal description with the Equalization Department's electronic records. A mismatch stops certification until the Equalization Department or local assessor approves the description.
  • For a deed made from a combined or divided parcel, the "parent" parcel's taxes are checked too.
  • For a land split, ask the local assessor whether a split is allowed, then bring the Land Split Certification Form and $5.00 to the treasurer. The fee is kept whether the certification is approved or denied.
  • A split is denied if taxes are delinquent. Public Act 23 of 2019 put this duty on county treasurers.

Plan ahead on timing. Ask for the certification early in the sale, because a legal description mismatch has to be cleared with the Equalization Department or the assessor first, and that step can take longer than the treasurer's own review. Bring the deed or the land split form, along with the $5.00 fee for a split, and keep a copy of the approved certificate for the closing file.

Selling with taxes owed

Check the parcel number on your deed against the county's online record, then confirm with the treasurer that nothing is delinquent. A clean certificate keeps the deed moving at closing. If a balance exists, ask the treasurer for a payoff figure so it can be settled from the sale proceeds.

The condition of the house changes none of this. A home with deferred repairs or tenants in place needs the same certificate, because the record belongs to the parcel number and legal description on file with the Equalization Department. If the legal description on your deed differs from the county's, resolve that with the assessor before the closing date, since the treasurer will not certify a deed that fails to match. A cash buyer still needs that certificate, so the same steps apply to a quick sale.

When do Lenawee County taxes go to the county treasurer?

On March 1. Unpaid bills from the townships and cities pass to the county through settlement that day. Before then, current winter taxes are paid to your local treasurer through the end of February.

Does the Lenawee County treasurer accept credit cards?

Yes, along with cash, checks, cashier's checks and money orders. Card payments carry an enhanced access fee. Delinquent bills can also be paid by phone through the county's BS&A system.

Where is the Lenawee County treasurer's office?

At 301 N. Main Street in Adrian. Hours are 8:00 a.m. to noon and 1:00 p.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays, and the office closes for lunch between noon and 1:00 p.m.

What does a Lenawee County tax certificate cover?

Five years of taxes. The treasurer confirms that all taxes on the parcel are paid for that period, using the parcel number and legal description on the deed.

No. Bidding ran from August 11, 2026, with payment due by noon on August 13. Ask the county treasurer about any parcels offered later.

Who handles property tax in Livingston County?

Three layers share the work. Each city or township assessor sets the value of a parcel. The county Equalization Department checks those assessments for uniformity and reports equalized values. The local city or township treasurer bills the current summer and winter taxes, and the Livingston County Treasurer takes over collection once taxes turn delinquent.

Know which office to ring. Your current summer or winter amount lives with the local city or township treasurer, so a bill question for a Howell house goes to a different desk than one for a Genoa Township house. The county treasurer also handles tax clearance of deeds and charges $2.50 to view a parcel's tax history online, a fee that cannot be taken by phone request.

  • County Treasurer: (517) 546-7010, weekdays 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., at 200 E Grand River Ave, Howell.
  • Equalization Department: (517) 546-4182, weekdays 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., at 304 E Grand River Ave, Howell.
  • Current bill, due dates and payment: your city or township treasurer.
  • Valuation or exemption question: your city or township assessor.

The county had a 2020 population of 193,866 and 78,441 housing units, of which 5.3 percent were vacant. Howell is the county seat, and many residents commute along I-96, US 23 and M-59.

How taxable value is calculated

Each bill starts from taxable value, a figure that can sit far below what the house would sell for. The county Equalization Department publishes a short glossary of how the numbers connect, and it explains why two neighbors with identical houses can pay very different bills.

Value terms used by the Livingston County Equalization Department
TermMeaning
Assessed value50 percent of the usual selling price, or true cash value
State equalized valueAssessed value after county and state equalization; usually equal to assessed value
Capped valueLast year's taxable value, less losses, raised by inflation or 5 percent (whichever is less), plus additions
Taxable valueThe lesser of state equalized value or capped value

Losses are parts of a property physically removed, such as a garage. Additions are parts physically added, such as a finished basement or a new family room. A homeowner who has held a property for many years usually has a taxable value well below the state equalized value, because the cap grows more slowly than market prices.

What happens to the tax bill after a sale?

The cap lifts. In the year following a transfer of ownership, taxable value is uncapped and equals the state equalized value. The capped formula resumes the next year and runs until the next transfer. A buyer who sees the seller's old tax bill should not assume it will stay that low.

The buyer must file a property transfer affidavit with the assessor in the city or township where the home sits within 45 days. Failing to file can bring a fine of $5 a day, up to $200. Sellers who want a smooth closing can remind the buyer's agent of this step, since the affidavit also tells the assessor who should receive the next bill.

  • Seller's side: tax history from the county treasurer, a payoff of any delinquent balance, and the title company's tax proration.
  • Buyer's side: the transfer affidavit, a request for the principal residence exemption if the home will be a primary residence, and an estimate of the uncapped bill.
  • Both: confirm whether special assessments are attached to the parcel.

How to appeal your assessment

Michigan appeals begin locally. If you believe the assessor has valued your home above half of its true cash value, take the question to the city or township Board of Review in March, then to the Michigan Tax Tribunal if you are still unsatisfied. Individual appeals are heard at that local level. The county Equalization Department can supply Board of Review information, appraisal study results, assessment roll data, equalized values and taxable values on request.

For parcel-level data, call (517) 546-4182 or email equalization@livgov.com to get an order number. The office is at 304 E Grand River Ave in Howell and is open weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. except county holidays. Bulk digital exports are priced at $0.04 per parcel, with a small per-sort addition for custom exports.

Equalization also keeps top-ten taxpayer information and State Tax Commission forms. The annual equalization and apportionment reports are posted on the county site for each year.

Unpaid taxes and foreclosure

The county treasurer is the collector of all delinquent real property taxes. Michigan's process runs three years. A parcel is forfeited to the county treasurer when its real property taxes are in the second year of delinquency, and taxes still unpaid on March 31 of the third year are foreclosed by the county as foreclosing governmental unit. People with an interest in the property at the time may claim excess proceeds from a sale, within statutory deadlines.

Before listing, ask the Livingston County Treasurer for a written payoff before listing, because interest and fees grow the longer a balance sits. Most closings clear the balance from the proceeds.

Many owners with back taxes also have a mortgage in arrears or an inherited house they cannot keep up. Selling for cash can end the problem before the forfeiture year, and the purchase price covers the payoff at closing.

Back taxes do not disappear when the house changes hands. They are paid from the sale proceeds or the title company will not close, so a seller who learns the figure early has time to plan.

Exemptions that can lower a bill

Two are listed: the homeowner's principal residence percentage, which is the part of a home you own and occupy that is exempt from certain school taxes, and the qualified agricultural exemption for property used mainly for farming. A new owner should ask the local assessor how and by when to claim the principal residence exemption for the home.

Michigan's constitution requires uniform assessment of property and caps assessed value at 50 percent of true cash value, which is why the numbers on a bill look lower than a sale price. A buyer comparing a Livingston County listing with a similar one in another state should start from taxable value when estimating the yearly bill.

Other relief, such as hardship relief, is handled by the local assessing unit. Ask that office before the March Board of Review window.

Pull together the last few tax bills, your deed and any special assessment notices ahead of time. Buyers' agents request all three, and having them in hand shortens the stretch between an accepted offer and closing.

Frequently asked questions

Who sends the Livingston County property tax bill?

Your city or township treasurer does. The county treasurer collects only after taxes turn delinquent, so ask the local treasurer for current summer and winter amounts.

How is taxable value different from state equalized value in Livingston County?

Taxable value is the lesser of state equalized value and capped value. The cap limits yearly growth to inflation or 5 percent, whichever is lower, until the property transfers.

Does my Livingston County tax bill go up when I buy a house?

It can. Taxable value is uncapped in the year after a transfer and equals state equalized value, then the cap resumes. File the property transfer affidavit within 45 days.

Where do I appeal my Livingston County assessment?

Start with the Board of Review in your city or township in March. If that does not resolve it, the Michigan Tax Tribunal is the next step. The county Equalization Department can provide supporting data.

How long before Livingston County can foreclose for unpaid taxes?

Michigan's process spans three years. Parcels forfeit in the second year of delinquency, and unpaid real property taxes at March 31 of the third year are foreclosed.

Which Macomb County office handles which part of the bill?

Three layers split the work. The assessor in each city, township or village sets the assessment. That municipality's treasurer mails the bill and collects it, as MCL 211.44 describes. The Macomb County Treasurer enters the picture only when taxes go unpaid past the local deadline.

The county had 881,217 people in 2020, spread over 27 cities, townships and villages. Warren, Sterling Heights and St. Clair Shores are cities, and Armada, New Haven and Romeo are villages. A buyer in Roseville and a buyer in Romeo therefore receive bills from different offices, even though the county treasurer sits behind both.

The county Treasurer's Office answers at 586-469-5190 or treasurer@macombgov.org, weekdays 8:00 a.m. to 4:15 p.m. Its tax information page separates real property, meaning land and permanent structures, from personal property such as machinery, fixtures and equipment owned by a business. Delinquent real or personal property tax can be paid online with a debit card or ACH, and a GIS search returns legal descriptions from an address or tax ID.

How to appeal your assessment

Start with the local board of review, because the county cannot change an individual assessment. The Macomb County Equalization Department (586-469-5260, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.) runs sales and appraisal studies by property class in each city and township to check that local assessments are fair across the county. Its authority is Section 211.34 of the General Property Tax Act.

A protest starts at the board of review, whose first March meeting falls on the second Monday, or the Tuesday or Wednesday after if the local government chose that. Under MCL 211.30 it must hold at least 12 hours of hearings that week, including three hours after 6 p.m. Nonresidents may protest by letter, and local governments may extend that option to residents.

The written decision arrives by the first Monday in June and points to the Michigan Tax Tribunal as the next step, with a filing date printed on the notice. Keep that notice. If you miss the March session, the next opening is the following March.

Will a sale raise the next tax bill?

Usually yes. A long-held home carries a taxable value held down by an annual cap, and a sale lifts that value to the state equalized value, which tracks about half the market price, for the next year. The mechanics are in MCL 211.27a. The buyer, not the seller, files the change notice with the assessor, and has 45 days to do it.

Not every transfer counts as a sale for this purpose. The statute exempts:

  • Moves between spouses.
  • Residential transfers to a parent, child, sibling or grandchild that stay non-commercial.
  • Foreclosure transfers, until the lender resells.
  • Court-ordered transfers with no stated price.

For a seller, this means the buyer's carrying cost can differ sharply from yours, and a seller who owned for decades may want to tell a buyer to expect a higher bill. The assessor in your own city or township can quote the current taxable value, and the county Treasurer's tax histories show what has been paid. Sellers handling an estate should check whether the heir is a close relative under the statute, since that decides whether the taxable value resets when title moves out of the decedent's name.

Delinquent taxes and county fees

On March 1 following the tax year, unpaid real property tax becomes payable to the County Treasurer, with a 4% administration fee and interest at 1% per month. Forfeiture a year later raises the rate to 1.5% per month, applied back to the original delinquency date.

The county describes the sequence as a three-year forfeiture and foreclosure process. The schedule for 2025 taxes shows how the notices and fees stack up, and later tax years follow the same pattern:

Macomb County Treasurer schedule for unpaid property taxes
WhenWhat happens
March 1 after the tax yearTaxes delinquent, 4% fee and 1% interest added
June 1 and September 1First class mail notices
October 1$15 fee added
March 1 the following yearForfeiture, $175 minimum title search fee
September 1 that yearPersonal visit, $50 fee
January, third yearShow cause hearing with the Treasurer
March 31, third yearForeclosure final, redemption ends

A circuit court hearing in February of the third year produces the foreclosure judgment, and a $35 publication fee is added the November before.

How many warnings come before foreclosure?

An owner should receive all of these before foreclosure:

  • Four first class mail notices.
  • Two certified mail notices.
  • Three notices published in a county newspaper.
  • Staff visits to the property beginning each September, repeated until the redemption period expires.

The Treasurer's Office also offers to explain the process, set up a payment plan or point owners to assistance programs through its tax foreclosure prevention page.

Once foreclosure is final, the owner cannot get the property back. It is offered first to the State of Michigan at fair market value, then to the local community, and what remains goes to public auction held between the third Tuesday in July and the first Tuesday in November, with notice published 30 days ahead.

Money left over after an auction can belong to the former owner. For auctions beginning in 2021, anyone who held an interest at the time of foreclosure may file a claim for proceeds above the taxes owed. The county is also taking part in a settlement of claims for surplus proceeds from auctions before 2021, listed on the Treasurer's page as the Fox class action. For 2025 taxes, the claim deadline is July 1, 2028.

Selling with back taxes

Request a payoff figure from the Treasurer that runs through the planned closing date, and let the title company settle it out of the seller's proceeds. Interest at 1% per month keeps growing in the first year, so a payoff quoted for the first of a month changes the next month.

The register of deeds will record a warranty deed only with a Treasurer's certificate showing no unpaid tax for the preceding five years, under MCL 211.135. A seller who is still in the first delinquent year has the most room to act, because forfeiture fees such as the $175 title search charge have not yet been added.

Michigan also allows a collecting unit to add up to a 1% administration fee on bills paid before February 15 and a 3% late penalty from February 15 until the bill is returned as delinquent, if the municipality has authorized it. Ask your own city or township treasurer what it charges.

Frequently asked questions

When does Macomb County treat property tax as delinquent?

March 1 of the year after the tax year. A 4% fee and 1% interest are added at that point, and interest keeps running each month.

Who sets my Macomb County property assessment?

Your city or township assessor does. The county Equalization Department at 586-469-5260 compares assessments across the county but leaves individual assessments to local boards.

How long until Macomb County forecloses on unpaid property tax?

About three years. Property is forfeited after the first year, and unpaid taxes as of March 31 in the third year of delinquency lead to foreclosure and title passing to the county treasurer.

Does selling change my Macomb County taxable value?

The seller's value does not carry over to the buyer. After a transfer of ownership, the next year's taxable value is set at the state equalized value, and the buyer reports the transfer to the assessor within 45 days.

Can I recover auction proceeds after a Macomb County tax foreclosure?

Possibly. Former owners and others with an interest can file to claim proceeds above the taxes owed, under the county's published deadlines, and a separate class action settlement covers auctions before 2021.

Who handles property tax in Mecosta County

Due dates and penalties

Bills for the summer levy are mailed in the first week of July and can be paid without penalty through September 14. The winter bill follows in December. Under MCL 211.44(2), a bill that is lost or never received does not cancel the tax, so ask the township, city or village if nothing arrives.

WhenWhat happens

What happens if taxes go unpaid

The path runs through forfeiture to foreclosure. Roughly 23 months of delinquency ends in foreclosure, with title moving to the State of Michigan, because the state is Mecosta County's foreclosing governmental unit. The state auctions the parcel, and the sale results appear on Tax-Sale.info.

When an auction brings in more than what was owed, the former owner may claim the surplus. File Form 5743 with the state by the July 1 after the foreclosure date, wait for the state's response, then ask the circuit court for payment between February 1 and May 15.

If you are a few months behind, March 1 is the date to beat. Ask the treasurer for a payoff figure and, if you plan to sell, close before the parcel hits forfeiture.

How a sale changes the taxes on a house

A sale usually raises the taxable value. Year over year, taxable value may rise by no more than 5 percent or the inflation rate, whichever is less, but a change of ownership removes that limit and sets taxable value equal to the state equalized value the next year (MCL 211.27a). A long-time owner's bill can therefore look quite different on the buyer's first statement.

Some changes of hands leave the cap alone, among them transfers between spouses, certain residential transfers to a parent, child, sibling or grandchild who will not use the property commercially, and a foreclosure until the lender resells. The new owner has 45 days to tell the assessor, and the Property Transfer Affidavit is Form 2766 on the county's Equalization forms page.

Sellers who claimed the principal residence exemption should withdraw it after they move. The same page offers Form 2602 for that request and Form 2368 for the buyer's homestead affidavit. Farmland owners will also find the farmland exemption claim (Form 2599) and the qualified agricultural property affidavit (Form 3676) there.

How to appeal your assessment

Begin at the Board of Review in your township or city, which meets the week of the second Monday in March (MCL 211.30). The week must include at least 12 hours of sessions, some after 6 p.m. You may protest in person, send an agent, or write a letter where the local unit has allowed that.

The board owes written notice of its decision by the first Monday in June. An owner who still disagrees can petition the Michigan Tax Tribunal: July 31 of the tax year for residential and agricultural property, May 31 for commercial and industrial (MCL 205.735a). A residential owner generally must have protested to the Board of Review first.

Questions about one assessment go to the township hall, and the Equalization page keeps a list of township assessors. A few examples of hall details:

  • Colfax, hall at 14428 157th Ave., meets the third Wednesday at 6 p.m.
  • Grant, hall at 14982 21 Mile Rd., meets the second Monday at 6:30 p.m.
  • Hinton, hall at 9013 3 Mile Rd., Lakeview, meets the second Monday at 7 p.m.
  • Millbrook, hall at 3015 Jackson Rd., Blanchard, meets the first Monday at 7 p.m. and keeps office hours by appointment

The villages of Mecosta and Stanwood meet the first Monday at 6 p.m. and the second Monday at 7 p.m. respectively. Other townships keep their own websites.

Property taxes at closing

Closing usually includes a proration of the current bill, and for a warranty deed the county treasurer must certify that five years of taxes are paid (MCL 211.135). Afterward the register of deeds in Big Rapids records the deed and the assessors learn of the transfer.

A typical house in the county is valued near $178,900, but the real bill turns on the township, village and school district millage on each parcel. A short checklist before closing:

  • Ask the township or city treasurer for the current balance, and the county treasurer for any delinquent amount.
  • Find the parcel's millage in the county's published millage rates for the year.
  • Rescind any principal residence exemption after the sale.
  • Give the buyer the date by which the transfer affidavit is due.

Selling with taxes owed

You can still sell a house with a delinquent balance. The title company pays the county treasurer or local treasurer out of your proceeds, and the payoff figure should be requested a few days before closing so interest is counted to the right day. Waiting past the forfeiture date adds the higher interest rate and a long road to foreclosure, so earlier is cheaper.

A cash sale can skip lender appraisals and repair negotiations, which helps when a tax deadline is close. Even then the balance is settled at closing and the title company needs the treasurer's payoff.

Frequently asked questions

What is the deadline for the summer tax bill in Mecosta County?

September 14 is the last penalty-free day. Winter bills follow in December, and after February 14 townships may add 3 percent through the end of that month. March 1 sends anything unpaid to the county treasurer.

What does a late Mecosta County bill cost?

Interest of 1 percent a month starts after September 14 on the summer bill. At the county treasurer, a 4 percent administration charge is added, and interest climbs to 1.5 percent a month after forfeiture.

When does Mecosta County property reach tax foreclosure?

After roughly 23 months of delinquency. Forfeiture comes after the first year, and the State of Michigan then auctions the foreclosed parcel.

Does the county or my township decide what my house is worth?

The township or city assessor decides it. Equalization at the county measures whether each unit assesses at 50 percent of true cash value but does not value individual homes.

Can I recover surplus from a Mecosta County tax sale?

Yes, when the auction price exceeds the debt. File Form 5743 by July 1 after the foreclosure date, then make a circuit court motion between February 1 and May 15.

Which offices handle property tax

  • Local treasurer: current summer and winter bills for your city, village or township.
  • Local assessor: the value on your bill and any exemption questions.
  • Business personal property: the treasurer's second line, 248-858-0622.

For the fourteen units the county assesses, Equalization keeps separate lines: 248-858-8793 for property transfers and homestead claims, and 248-858-0776 for appraisal records and tax descriptions. Use them if you sold or bought recently and the bill still shows the earlier owner.

Equalization works across 52 assessing jurisdictions, adjusting each class of property so they all reach a common level of valuation. The division also decides homestead exemption questions, reassesses ownership transfers and reviews millage rollback calculations. For fourteen units, including Novi Township, Lyon Township, South Lyon, Pontiac and Rochester, it acts as the assessor itself and takes all assessment questions.

Oakland County for a home seller

Oakland County is a large Metro Detroit county with 1,288,337 residents. Housing is mostly owner-occupied, at 72.7%, and the median owner-occupied home is valued at $343,600. Median household income runs $97,760, and median gross rent is $1,376. The county counted 569,537 housing units in 2025.

Because the county is so large, ask the local assessor which school and special districts apply to your parcel, since the millage total depends on them.

How taxes are calculated and appealed

A bill equals taxable value divided by 1,000 and multiplied by the millage total for the parcel's taxing units. Assessed value is about half of market value, and taxable value is capped at the lesser of assessed value or the prior year's taxable value times the inflation multiplier, with a 5% ceiling. A change of ownership removes the cap for the following year.

Valuation appeals begin at the local March Board of Review. Michigan law gives owners one chance a year to challenge a residential value there, and the Michigan Tax Tribunal is the next step, with residential petitions due July 31 after a March appearance. File the petition with the board of review for your city or township.

Relief programs sit mostly with the local unit. Cities such as Novi publish a hardship exemption application and a summer tax deferral process, and the county treasurer offers repayment help once a balance is delinquent.

Do not wait for the final notice, because fees and the 18% interest on forfeited parcels keep adding up each month.

Order an official delinquent tax statement before you list. Title companies, owners and others can buy one through the county's Property Gateway system, and it shows what the county treasurer holds against the parcel. The local treasurer will give you the current-year balance separately.

At the Register of Deeds, a warranty deed or any deed with a warranty clause needs a tax certification from the county treasurer, which costs $5. That certification confirms taxes are up to date. If back taxes are owed, the title company pays them from the seller's proceeds so the certification can issue and the deed can be recorded. See the county's Register of Deeds guide for recording costs.

A cash buyer does not need a lender's approval, which can make it practical to clear a delinquency quickly at closing, but the payoff still comes out of your proceeds and the statement still has to be bought first.

Who do I pay in Oakland County if my tax is current?

Pay your city, village or township treasurer. The county treasurer takes payment once a bill has become delinquent, and its portal can handle both kinds in the same system.

March 31, 2027. That date is the last day to pay unpaid 2024 and earlier taxes and keep the property. Foreclosure takes effect April 1.

The county portal adds 3.5% on debit and credit cards. An eCheck or ACH payment costs $2.50.

Does the county or my city decide my home's value?

Your city or township assessor sets it, except in fourteen units where the county Equalization Division is the assessor. The county equalizes values among all 52 assessing jurisdictions.

Whom do I ask about a Saginaw County tax bill?

Three layers touch each tax bill in this county. The assessor of your city or township sets the value, the local treasurer there mails the bill, and the County Treasurer steps in once taxes fall behind. Because Michigan keeps assessing local, the contact printed on your notice answers questions about value or timing faster than any county number.

Go to Room 107 at 111 S. Michigan in Saginaw (48602) or call (989) 790-5225 between 8:00 and 5:00 on weekdays. This is the office that collects every delinquent real property bill. It also manages the Delinquent Tax Revolving Fund and the county's hotel and motel tax, and its treasurer chairs the Land Bank Authority that holds tax foreclosed parcels. Regular summer and winter dates are set locally, so ask the treasurer of your own municipality.

  • Value, exemptions and the spring appeal: your local assessor.
  • Current bills: the local treasurer named on the statement.
  • Past-due balances and tax certificates: the county treasurer, (989) 790-5225.
  • Deed recording: the register of deeds, (989) 790-5270.

How are Saginaw County properties valued, and how do owners appeal?

Michigan sets assessments at half of true cash value. The figure that gets multiplied by the millage, taxable value, climbs by the smaller of 5% or the inflation rate each year until a sale resets it (MCL 211.27a). Your assessment notice shows both numbers.

Each local board of review opens on the second Monday of March and must sit at least 12 hours during that week, with evening time included (MCL 211.30). A written ruling follows before the first Monday of June, and it explains the next step to the Michigan Tax Tribunal. A township or city can also allow protests by letter, and a nonresident owner can file by letter regardless.
